content: The systematic review and meta-analysis published in PLOS Medicine in 2014 examined the relationship between water, sanitation, hygiene, and soil-transmitted helminth infections. Another study by Ziegelbauer et al. in 2012 focused on the impact of sanitation on soil-transmitted helminth infections, also using a systematic review and meta-analysis approach. Boateng et al. (2012) proposed a research agenda targeting the control and elimination of helminth diseases in humans, emphasizing the need for integrated strategies. Gazzinelli et al. (2012) explored the social ecology, environmental determinants, and health systems influencing helminth diseases, while Lustigman et al. (2012) addressed the broader challenges of helminthiasis in humans. Welch et al. (2016) investigated the effects of deworming in non-pregnant adolescent and adult women, as outlined in the PROSPERO database. The WHO guidelines recommend preventive chemotherapy to control soil-transmitted helminth infections in at-risk populations, including children and women of reproductive age. Gopaldas et al. (1983) studied the nutritional impact of anti-parasitic drugs, vitamin A, and iron-folic acid supplementation on underprivileged schoolgirls in India. In the Philippines, Insetta et al. (2014) identified fear of birth defects as a significant barrier to soil-transmitted helminth treatment among pregnant women. Boselli et al. (2011) demonstrated the effectiveness of integrating deworming into existing immunization and vitamin A supplementation campaigns in Lao PDR, highlighting its cost-effectiveness. Casey et al. (2011) found that weekly iron-folic acid supplementation combined with regular deworming was a cost-effective strategy to prevent anemia in women of reproductive age in Vietnam. Salam et al. (2015) reviewed the effects of administering anthelmintics during pregnancy, while Larocque et al. (2005) explored the relationship between soil-transmitted helminth infection intensity and anemia during pregnancy. A subsequent trial by Larocque et al. (2006) in Peru evaluated the impact of antenatal mebendazole on reducing low birth weight in hookworm-endemic areas. The WHO's 2016 recommendations on antenatal care aim to enhance pregnancy outcomes, including addressing helminth infections. Means et al. (2016) reviewed the effects of anthelmintics on HIV disease progression in helminth-endemic areas. Jia et al. (2012) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on soil-transmitted helminth reinfection following drug treatment. The WHO's 2015 report emphasized the role of improved water, sanitation, and hygiene in enhancing nutrition outcomes. The organization also highlighted the importance of school-based interventions to reduce helminth infections as part of health-promoting school initiatives. The WHO Model Lists of Essential Medicines (2017) and the International Pharmacopoeia (2015) provide guidance on essential treatments, including anthelmintics. The GRADE guidelines, developed by Guyatt et al. (2011, 2008), offer a systematic approach to evaluating evidence quality and making healthcare recommendations. Taylor-Robinson et al. (2007, 2012) and Dickson et al. (2000) reviewed the effects of deworming drugs on growth, cognitive performance, and nutritional indicators in children. Awasthi et al. (2013) conducted a large-scale trial in North India, assessing the impact of biannual albendazole deworming on preschool children. Aiken et al. (2015) reanalyzed the health and educational impacts of a school-based deworming program in Kenya. Gulani et al. (2007) systematically reviewed the effects of intestinal anthelmintic drugs on hemoglobin levels, while Watson et al. (2009) examined the role of deworming in delaying HIV disease progression. The WHO's 2014 handbook for guideline development and the GRADE Evidence to Decision frameworks (2016) provide structured methodologies for healthcare decision-making. The WHO Steering Group and Guideline Development Groups, comprising experts in nutrition, public health, and clinical practice, have contributed to the development of evidence-based recommendations for controlling soil-transmitted helminth infections in at-risk populations.
